record.note: AN OPEN-SIDED WAGON SHED BESIDE THE FRONT GABLE, and the picture is the whole reason it is here. The verified Trowbridge/Gale 1902 plate (data/sources/trowbridge_green_tree_1902.json), captioned 1835, shows an open-sided wagon shed attached at the left of the house with a covered wagon standing under it — a tier-5 retrospective view, which may drive furniture and setting and may never drive a coordinate. WHICH WALL IS DERIVED: the existing north (+u) host wall is unchanged. T-2376 places the bay at that wall's front end, ending at the same +v plane as the native primary entrance, instead of its former rear-end station. The covered wagon shares this centre. This is reconstructed setting from a retrospective drawing, not a surveyed coordinate or proof of the exact July-1835 state; the inn and its doors do not move. The canonical low connector and farther gabled range are independent building geometry. The unadopted prepared Andreas reading closes the shoulder; this open wagon bay remains separate native yard geometry, not the gabled range. HOW BIG IS ARITHMETIC on numbers already here: the bay is 4.05 m along the wall (the wagon's body and 0.50 m of air at each end) by 3.20 m out from it (the ground a parked wagon is given), its open eave stands 2.95 m up (0.35 m over the tilt it covers) and its plate meets the wall 3.63 m up at 12 degrees. What is invented is that this inn had a wagon shed on 1 July 1835 and every dimension of it: docs/LIBERTIES.md L134. NOT THE SAME THING as the low one-storey additions John Gray describes at each end of the house — those are attributes of the BUILDING, dated three to six years after the scene and deliberately excluded from its footprint; this is a yard structure on the yard's own ground, and it does not date them.

THE COVERED WAGON UNDER THE SHED, from the same plate and standing on the same derived centre as the bay over it. It is the farm wagon this record already draws — the body, the wheels and the tongue are L131's invented numbers and have not moved — with a TILT added: canvas on bows, 1.10 m of rise over the body's top rail and 0.12 m pulled past the end bows, open at both ends. The bows themselves are not drawn, for the reason the barrels' hoops are not: under the canvas there is nothing to see. It lies ALONG the wall because that is how a 4.05 m bay takes a 3.05 m body, with the tongue down and out of the open end into the yard. What is invented is the wagon, the tilt and the fact that either stood here on 1 July 1835: docs/LIBERTIES.md L131 and L134.
